primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's autobiographical response to testimonials, built around two stories, one fictional and one true, whose shared moral is 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep doing my best and God will do the rest'

His account of a poor childhood in postwar Sampaloc -- hawking newspapers, selling cigarettes and shining shoes, sleeping on sidewalks -- and a purely secular public-school education that left him without religious instruction

How his early frustrations proved blessings in disguise: poverty taught him the value of hard work and scholarships, a father's insistence turned him to law, and the Yale scholarship he could not afford led him to found his own travel agency

Far Eastern University as the turning point that gave him academic excellence, a liberal education, leadership, his Catholic faith and his wife Leni -- and the long road from declined government offers to the Supreme Court and the chief justiceship
sub_topics: He thanks friends for their testimonials and announces two stories, the first fictional and the second real and true
The medieval parable of the farmer whose runaway horse, eleven horses, lamed son and spared conscription each drew the same reply: 'Good news, bad news, who knows?'
His own beginnings: born poor, the youngest of four, his father supporting seven siblings as well, having left school to work as a rank-and-file government employee
Postwar hardship in Sampaloc -- hawking newspapers, selling cigarettes, shining shoes, sleeping on sidewalks waiting for the morning delivery, and calling out the names of the dailies in the streets
A purely secular education at Candaba Elementary, Juan Luna Elementary and Mapa High School, with no catechism and parents not steeped in their faith
His ambition to be a chemical engineer overridden by his father's insistence on law -- 'Pilosopo ka kasi, matigas ang ulo' -- in a time when a father's word was law
The UP scholarship he could not use because his father could not afford the 15-centavo bus fare to Diliman, sending him instead to FEU within walking distance
Supporting his studies by peddling textbooks to classmates and selling bibles to professors
The Yale master's scholarship secured on Dean Jovito R. Salonga's recommendation, lost for want of plane fare after a Smith Mundt grant was denied -- a moment of frustration and defeat

The four blessings in disguise: poverty taught hard work, yielding a cum laude degree and sixth place in the 1960 bar despite hospitalization; big dreams led to the presidency of a leading newspaper; the lost Yale trip produced Baron Travel Corporation in 1967; and his five children obtained the Ivy League graduate degrees he never did

FEU's demanding professors -- Francisco M. Africa on logic and debate, Benito F. Reyes on philosophy, Angelica Mendoza on botany and Rosario P. Melchor on grammar and style, whose rules he still applied in writing Supreme Court decisions
The FEU law faculty of leading lawyers and young Ivy League graduates, and administrators like Don Angel Palanca and treasurer Hector 'Mang Etoy' del Rosario

Dean Alejandro R. Roces, who taught him 'the art of knowing everything about something and something about everything,' advised the NUSP he founded, coached his campus campaigns and became his wedding ninong

President Teodoro Evangelista's view of education as a means to a life of the mind and spirit, and the lesson that liberal education and specialization must go hand in hand -- which later gave him confidence to decide cases involving new sciences and paradigms

His search for God: Fr. Michael Nolan recruiting him into FEU Student Catholic Action, Fr. James Sheehy's teaching that a good Catholic must lead others to purity, and his renewal in Bukas Loob sa Diyos with Leni in the mid-1980s
Lay leadership: delegate to the Second Plenary Council of the Philippines in 1991 and, appointed by Pope John Paul II, the only Filipino member of the Pontifical Council for the Laity for 1996-2001

Leadership at FEU turning a shy lad into president of the FEU Central Student Organization and co-founder and president of the NUSP, where he met Elenita A. Carpio of St. Scholastica's, who became his wife
Declining early government offers from Executive Secretary Rafael Salas and Justice Leo A. Quisumbing because the pay could not see his children through school

The 1992 meeting with President-elect Fidel V. Ramos, whom he had known since 1983 in the Rotary Club of Manila: he declined a Cabinet post, having voted for Salonga, and accepted instead the promise of a Supreme Court seat, which came in 1995

His selection by President Arroyo from the JBC short list to succeed Chief Justice Davide, the announcement reaching him mid-speech at a Pan Pacific Hotel dinner, and his ultimate dream of being welcomed at the pearly gates

stances.claim: Neither good fortune nor bad can be judged at the moment it arrives; the right response is the farmer's -- to keep doing one's best and let God do the rest -- because a series of apparent bad news may turn out, in time, to have been good news after all.
stances.rhetorical_move: parable first, then autobiography as the test case: a fictional story supplies the moral that his own life is then shown to confirm

stances.claim: Poverty and early frustration were blessings in disguise, because they taught him the value of hard work and a good education, drove him to dream big, and redirected him into ventures and achievements he would not otherwise have attempted.
stances.rhetorical_move: numbered retrospective reframing -- 'First... Second... Third...' -- turning each setback into a named benefit

stances.claim: Excellence in a profession is not enough: a lawyer must also have a good grasp of the arts, history, literature, ethics and the humanities, and it was this liberal education that later gave him the confidence to decide cases involving avant-garde sciences, new economic paradigms and ultramodern technology.
stances.rhetorical_move: crediting named teachers and then drawing a general principle about legal education from their example

stances.claim: He kept his distance from political office -- declining a technical assistantship, a judgeship and a Cabinet post, and accepting a Supreme Court seat precisely because it was not political -- and waited until his children's education was secure before entering public service.
stances.rhetorical_move: first-person recollection of declined offers, used to establish independence from the appointing authority

notable_anecdotes: The medieval parable of the farmer whose horse ran away, returned with ten wild horses, lamed his son, and thereby spared the son from a war that killed every other young man in the village -- to each turn the farmer answered, 'Good news, bad news, who knows?'

As a boy he hawked newspapers, sold cigarettes and shone shoes in Sampaloc, sleeping on the sidewalk to wait for the dawn delivery and running through the streets shouting the names of the Manila dailies.
His father overruled his ambition to be a chemical engineer with 'Pilosopo ka kasi, matigas ang ulo' and the demand that he start something of his own rather than copy his siblings.

He won a UP scholarship with his high school classmates before the Oblation, but his father could not afford the 15-centavo bus fare to Diliman, so he enrolled at FEU, which was within walking distance.

Dean Salonga's recommendation won him a Yale master's scholarship, but with the Smith Mundt grant denied and no money for the plane fare he had to give it up -- a defeat that later inspired him to found Baron Travel Corporation.

At a dinner he hosted at the Pan Pacific Hotel, emcee Evelyn Toledo-Dumdum interrupted his speech to report that Channel 7 had announced his appointment as Chief Justice; he froze before the microphone for the first time in his life, and afterwards he and Leni went to church to thank the Lord.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' answered friends' testimonials with two stories, one fictional and one true. The first was a medieval parable of a farmer whose runaway horse, unexpected windfall of eleven horses, son's broken leg and consequent exemption from a fatal conscription each drew the same reply: 'Good news, bad news, who knows? I will just keep on doing my best and God will do the rest.' The second was CJP's own life. Born poor, the youngest of four children of a father who had left school to support seven siblings, he hawked newspapers, sold cigarettes and shone shoes in postwar Sampaloc, sleeping on sidewalks to wait for the dawn delivery, and received a purely secular education in public schools without catechism. His ambition to be a chemical engineer gave way to his father's insistence on law; a UP scholarship went unused because the family could not afford the bus fare to Diliman, so he enrolled at Far Eastern University nearby, funding his studies by peddling textbooks and selling bibles. A Yale scholarship won on Dean Salonga's recommendation was lost for want of plane fare. Each frustration, he recounted, proved a blessing in disguise: poverty taught him hard work, yielding a cum laude degree and sixth place in the 1960 bar; big dreams carried him to the presidency of a leading newspaper; the lost Yale trip produced Baron Travel Corporation; and his five children earned the Ivy League graduate degrees he had missed. FEU gave him demanding professors, the ideal of knowing everything about something and something about everything, lay Catholic faith through Columban priests, student leadership, and his wife Leni. He declined early government offers and a Cabinet post from President Ramos, accepting instead a Supreme Court seat in 1995, and learned of his appointment as Chief Justice mid-speech at a hotel dinner, freezing before the microphone for the first time in his life.
